prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic twist angle, establishing moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B017) as my preferred single-part prize, but after the first round I hold it less firmly and with a clearer view of what it would have to rest on. This is the one candidate on the list where I can judge the central theory first-hand: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model is an electronic-structure calculation that predicted a vanishing Dirac velocity and flat bands at a specific twist angle, and the prediction was made years before the experiment. Jarillo-Herrero's group then found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle, and the existence of these phases has been reproduced by many independent laboratories over about eight years. That is a prediction followed by a decisive experiment, and it has opened a tunable platform for correlated electrons in which twist and stacking act as a control parameter in many other materials. I would draw the citation on the prediction and on the observed phases, not on any pairing mechanism, which the committee agrees is unsettled. I accept the chair's observation that the dispute between B017 and B041 is about weighting, not about facts. I weigh field-creating novelty and a prediction-experiment chain more heavily than the cleaner allocation and greater maturity of the clocks, and that is a judgement about taste that colleagues may reasonably resolve differently. I have not changed my configuration, but I have changed my confidence, and I would not oppose B041 if it carries the committee.
statement.case_against: The reservations from round 1 stand and were reinforced by colleagues. The origin of the superconductivity is unresolved and sample-to-sample and twist-angle variation is large. Lindroth, Mehlig, Kroll and Pearce argue that this calls for a few more years, and I cannot dismiss that. The credit is also not exhaustive. Cao and Fatemi performed the 2018 measurements, Dean, Young, Kim and others established the hBN moire platform and later correlated states, and earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto and by Suarez Morell and colleagues bears on priority. Three names cannot cover this, and a citation can only partly compensate. By comparison B041 has a clean two-name allocation, independently confirmed accuracy near 1e-18 and no open question about whether the central result exists. If the committee concludes that maturity and attribution should decide, B041 is the defensible outcome, and my remaining objection to it is only the margin against the 2005 and 2012 prizes.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the magic-wavelength lattice concept is itself the citable discovery, separate from combs and ion traps, and that confirmed uncertainty below 1e-18 settles maturity regardless of the SI second.
responses.response: I find this a better argument than I allowed in round 1. If the citation is anchored on the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice, the overlap with the 2005 comb prize is a boundary question I can accept, and I withdraw the description of it as only a refinement of an honoured lineage. I still cannot judge Ye's credit from outside the field, and the chair's question on how much of it rests on the lattice clock rather than the comb programme is one that you and Lindroth are better placed to answer than I am. I do not think your Boulder disclosure calls for any action; a doctoral research stay in the environment where Ye's group grew, with no collaboration, is the kind of proximity every member of a small committee has somewhere.

responses.point: Lindroth lists B017 as an alternative but says the unresolved superconductivity mechanism and a possible later settlement argue for waiting, and she also asks whether the invention against discovery distinction should count against B041.
responses.response: On maturity, I draw the line between the existence of the phases and the explanation of them. A prize needs the first and does not need the second; the Academy has recognised discoveries whose mechanism was still debated. Where I agree with you is on sample dependence, which I regard as a real weakness and not only a pending phenomenology. On the distinction between invention and discovery, I do not think it should be a criterion by itself. The committee has honoured instruments and methods that opened new measurements, and the only honest question is whether the achievement changed what physicists can do or know. Both B041 and B017 do that, in different ways, and I think the distinction mostly restates the weighting dispute the chair has described.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks whether members who raised the SI redefinition consider it a reason to postpone, whether altermagnetism can compete in round 2, and he himself raises the doubt that Ye's credit rests partly on combs.
responses.response: I do not treat the missing SI redefinition as a reason to wait for B041, since the confirmed 1e-18 agreement already establishes the science. On altermagnetism, I have no new evidence of the kind your question asks for. The symmetry classification is a real conceptual advance, no other member ranks it first, the materials base is small and the priority questions with earlier symmetry-based work are open, so I do not argue that it should replace B041 or B017 in this round. I keep it as an alternative only because it is the strongest conceptual idea in my own field, and I would rather see it return in a later cycle with a firmer experimental record. On your point about Ye, I agree it is the main soft spot in B041 and the citation wording should carry the burden.

responses.point: Olsson regards the timing for B017 as appropriate for the originating discovery, judges field-creating novelty to outweigh the cleaner allocation of B041, and names Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Kim, Yazdani and Efetov as omitted.
responses.response: We agree on the substance, and your admission that B017 is not the safer prize is the honest framing. I would go slightly further on credit than you did: of those omitted, the 2018 first-author measurements by Cao and Fatemi are the most difficult gap, because they are the observations the citation names. If the committee takes B017 the citation must say plainly that it recognises the prediction and the discovery of the phases, and the discussion record should state that the three-person limit forces the omissions. If that gap appears too large, I would, as I said in round 1, accept B041 and would not regard it as a poor outcome.

responses.point: Johansson supports B041 with a citation built on the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, rejects an asymmetric use of the invention-versus-discovery distinction, and moves B004 to an alternative.
responses.response: Your point that the distinction must not be applied asymmetrically given earlier prizes for inventions is correct and I have taken it into my own answer above. I also appreciate that you reconsidered the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp set for B004, since the contested attribution there is the reason I did not rank B004 first either. I would add that the same standard should apply to B017: if the committee accepts that two named clock inventors leave Lemonde, Gill and Ludlow aside, it should accept that three named people leave Cao and Fatemi aside, and the two cases should be judged on the same footing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the pairing mechanism and the sample dependence of twisted bilayer graphene to be a question of maturity that argues for waiting, or only of later phenomenology.
Whether a three-name citation can credibly cover the 2018 experiments given that Cao and Fatemi are omitted and earlier twisted-bilayer theory has priority claims.

Whether the lattice-clock concept is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes and how much of Ye's credit rests on the lattice clock itself, which I cannot judge from outside precision spectroscopy.
Whether my recollection of the altermagnetism experimental timeline is accurate; I have not changed my view that it is early.
statement.conflict_note: No documented personal or institutional connection to MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero, Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. My own field of magnetism and electronic-structure theory is professionally close to B017, B019 and B008, which bears on expertise and not on any personal tie. I have read the round-1 disclosures: Kroll's Boulder stay, Pearce's astroparticle proximity, Johansson's circuit QED work, Lindroth's collaborations and Olsson's Chalmers and Japan ties. None in my view requires recusal on B017 or B041.
